transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-08-11
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Mark Chen (Harbor Insights, CTO), Leah Ortiz (Harbor Insights, ML Eng), Tom Reynolds (Product)
Link: https://redwood.ai/docs/hosted-api (shared)

[00:00] Alex Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex, AE at Redwood. With me is Priya our solutions engineer. How's everybody doing?
[00:06] Mark Chen: Good, thanks. Running on a tight schedule so we're hoping to see the hosted API basics and then talk about our latency concerns.
[00:12] Priya Singh: Great, we'll keep it tight. Quick agenda: a short quickstart on the Hosted API for chat/text, streaming behavior, important params, and then retries/idempotency and where caching and batching fit in; leave time for Q&A and POC next steps.
[00:24] Tom Reynolds: Sounds good. We mainly need a replacement for our current inference pipeline - currently call OpenAI for chat, but cost is creeping up and we need better control.
[00:33] Leah Ortiz: Also want to validate p99 latency for 512-token responses, and whether streaming helps our UX.
[00:39] Priya Singh: Totally. We'll demo a live call. A quick note, the playground in the console uses the same API under the hood - so what you see in console = hosted calls.

--- Demo setup / live API call ---
[02:05] Priya Singh: All right I'm switching to screen. I'll run a simple chat request: messages array, model equals redwood-... uh the model name is 'redwood-chat-1' for this demo; we set temperature 0.2, max_tokens 512, and enable streaming true.
[02:22] (keyboard clacking)
[02:30] Priya Singh: You'll see the response stream in chunks - that's server-sent events style, so your client can render token by token and improve perceived latency. Note that streaming doesn't change total compute but it improves time-to-first-byte.
[02:48] Mark Chen: Are there libraries for the stream client?
[02:52] Priya Singh: Yes - SDKs for Node/Python have streaming helpers. There's also a simple SSE/HTTP chunk example in the docs link I shared.

[03:20] Alex Martinez: On params: we covered temperature and max_tokens; top_p is supported as an alternative sampling knob - lower top_p tends to reduce hallucination in some workloads. The 'n' parameter returns multiple completions but multiplies cost. Stop tokens supported too for truncation.
[03:44] Leah Ortiz: How do you recommend we set those for assistant-style Q&A?
[03:48] Priya Singh: For Q&A we usually do temperature 0-0.3, top_p 0.9-1.0, and set max_tokens conservatively - also use structured output or function-calls if you want deterministic JSON.

[04:12] Tom Reynolds: What about retries? We get intermittent 503s today.
[04:16] Priya Singh: Good question. Hosted API recommends idempotency keys on mutating ops or long-running calls. For generation calls we surface a retryable status for transient errors - we suggest exponential backoff with jitter. We also expose a request_id in response headers to correlate attempts.
[04:34] Mark Chen: Any best practices so we don't duplicate outputs on retry?
[04:37] Priya Singh: Use idempotency keys if you're storing outputs server-side; in UI flows you can detect duplicates by matching request hash + idempotency. For streaming specifically, clients should reattach and resume from last ack point - we have examples in the runbook.

[05:12] Alex Martinez: On cost/latency tradeoffs: if you need ultra-low latency at high qps, teams often go Dedicated; Hosted is good for quick time-to-value and smaller scale. We can provide rough p95 numbers depending on model and token length.
[05:26] Leah Ortiz: Can you give an example p95 you see for 256 tokens on hosted?
[05:30] Priya Singh: It varies per model, but as a ballpark hosted p95 for 256 tokens is in the low hundreds of ms for smaller models, and for larger models it could be 700-1200ms depending on concurrency and batching. Important caveat: benchmarking depends on network, region, and model choice. We'll share benchmark script so you can run against your workload.

[06:05] Mark Chen: We care about data controls - does hosted keep input data? We need SOC2 plus ability to exclude retention.
[06:12] Alex Martinez: Hosted API supports configurable data retention policies; for enterprise we offer a no-retention option, plus SOC 2 Type II, SSO via SAML, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS integration for encryption at rest. For full private control you can look at Redwood Private.
[06:32] Tom Reynolds: Is KMS per-customer, or do you manage keys?
[06:36] Priya Singh: We support customer-managed keys (BYOK) via AWS KMS/HSM in Private or Dedicated; for hosted we also offer an enterprise option with customer keys - we'll include details in the security pack.

[07:05] Leah Ortiz: Can you speak to caching - prefix or KV cache?
[07:09] Priya Singh: Sure. We do prefix caching (we sometimes call it KV cache) - we cache repeated prefixes to avoid recomputing large context for high-volume repeated prompts. It's most effective when you have many similar requests or a stable system prompt. Cache hits reduce tokens billed in some cases and reduce latency. We also do workload-aware batching to improve throughput.
[07:35] Mark Chen: Would that break privacy?
[07:37] Priya Singh: Cache is per-tenant and optional; you can disable caching if needed. For shared multi-tenant hosted customers it's isolated at the account level.

[08:00] Alex Martinez: Quick note on quantization - that's more about Dedicated/Private runtime choices; hosted offers quantized model variants when appropriate but for strict accuracy you can pin the non-quantized model.

--- live code and example flows ---
[09:12] Priya Singh: I'm going to run a short script to show retries and idempotency: I'll intentionally throttle one request and show the request_id and backoff in logs.
[09:35] (terminal noises)
[09:42] Priya Singh: You can see here: request-id: rwd-27a1, status 502 then automatic retry with exponential backoff, second attempt returns 200 and payload.
[09:55] Leah Ortiz: Nice - do you expose metrics for retry counts per key?
[09:59] Priya Singh: Yes the Console traces requests; you can see retry counts, p50/p95 latencies, token usage per request, and cost breakdown by route.

[11:20] Mark Chen: About streaming - if we stream partial tokens for UI, and user cancels mid-stream, do we still get billed for full generation?
[11:28] Priya Singh: Billing is token-based on tokens actually generated. If you cancel the request client-side and the server stops generation, billing stops for tokens not generated. With streaming you can close the connection and the server will stop generating unless you have stored partial outputs on your side.

[12:05] Tom Reynolds: Any limits on concurrent streams?
[12:08] Alex Martinez: Hosted has rate limits by default but they are configurable for enterprise tiers; we can discuss quota increases. Also Dedicated gives reserved GPU capacity and higher sustained throughput guarantees.

[13:00] Leah Ortiz: If we start with Hosted and then move to Dedicated for scale, how smooth is the model/rollout?
[13:06] Priya Singh: Smooth - same API surface and model catalog. We provide routing policies so you can pin traffic to a Dedicated pool or fall back to Hosted. Model versioning and rollouts are supported in both.

[14:10] Mark Chen: Security review: we will need SOC2 docs, penetration test reports, and SSO setup guide.
[14:16] Alex Martinez: We'll put those in the security pack and share the SAML setup doc. Also we'll send the checklist for compliance.

[15:00] (brief silence as attendees skim docs)

--- Qualification and timeline ---
[16:05] Alex Martinez: Quick qual Qs: what's your expected QPS for the initial POC?
[16:10] Leah Ortiz: For proof-of-concept, we're aiming for 30 qps with median response sizes ~300 tokens. If POC looks good, we could scale to 200 qps within six weeks.
[16:22] Priya Singh: That's reasonable. For 30 qps hosted is fine; for sustained 200 qps we'd likely recommend Dedicated/reserved capacity for predictable latency. We'll size a Dedicated pool in the POC scoping call.

[17:05] Tom Reynolds: Success criteria: p95 latency under 800ms for 512 tokens, integrated SSO, and cost under $X per 1k tokens - kind of placeholder.
[17:17] Mark Chen: Yes, and deterministic JSON outputs for some product flows.

[18:00] Priya Singh: Deterministic outputs - function-calling or structured output with stop tokens and lower temperature helps. Also eval harnesses can detect regressions - Redwood Optimize can run quality checks on prompts over time.

[19:10] Alex Martinez: We'll include Redwood Optimize notes in the follow ups; it gives batching/quantization suggestions and monitors regressions on eval sets.

--- Q&A / edge cases raised ---
[22:05] Leah Ortiz: If we want to do zero-retention and customer-managed keys, is that available on Hosted?
[22:12] Alex Martinez: Yes for enterprise customers we can provision a no-retention plan and support BYOK. For absolute air-gapped needs we'd suggest Redwood Private.

[23:00] Mark Chen: Do you support regional routing - like EU-only?
[23:04] Priya Singh: Yes. We can restrict processing to region and support EU data residency. We'll note region in the POC spec.

[24:10] Tom Reynolds: Any gotchas around the streaming SDK for mobile clients?
[24:15] Priya Singh: Mobile clients should handle partial tokens and reassembly - use our token-level SSE helper or WebSocket if you need two-way. Also watch connection timeouts on certain mobile networks; we have reconnect patterns in docs.

[26:30] Alex Martinez: Let's talk about the POC timeline: we propose a 2-week POC - week 1 integration and baseline tests, week 2 performance testing and tuning. Deliverables: benchmark report, config recommendations for batching/cache, and go/no-go decision.

[27:10] Mark Chen: That aligns. We'll need pricing for both hosted usage during POC and an optional Dedicated quote for committed capacity.

[28:00] Alex Martinez: I'll send a Hosted vs Dedicated one-pager and pricing ranges after this call. Priya will share the benchmark script and runbook.

[30:05] Leah Ortiz: For the benchmark script can you include sample payloads and a way to simulate streaming reads?
[30:11] Priya Singh: Yes, we'll include a streaming client and an HTTP non-streaming client and guidance for how to measure time-to-first-byte vs time-to-last-byte, and how to capture p95/p99.

[32:20] (short technical tangent about tokenization differences)
[32:40] Priya Singh: One small note: different models tokenize differently; if you move models you'll want to re-evaluate token counts. That affects billing and max_tokens.

[34:00] Tom Reynolds: If we run the benchmark and see consistent timeouts at peak, do you help tune?
[34:06] Priya Singh: Yes SEs work with customers on tuning batch sizes, concurrency, and caching. For Dedicated we can tweak kernel scheduling and quantization recommendations.

[36:15] Mark Chen: Any legal docs to start? NDA or MSA?
[36:19] Alex Martinez: We'll share our standard NDA and an MSA template; legal can fast-track for POC.

[37:00] (wrap-up)
[37:05] Alex Martinez: Quick recap: we'll send pricing and Hosted vs Dedicated comparison, security pack (SOC2, SAML, KMS options), benchmark script + runbook, and schedule POC scoping for Aug 18.
[37:20] Mark Chen: Perfect. Who's doing what?
[37:24] Alex Martinez: Action items: Alex sends pricing and docs; Priya sends benchmark script; Leah provides sample dataset; we'll book the scoping call.
[37:35] Tom Reynolds: Thanks all.
[37:38] Leah Ortiz: Thanks.
[37:40] Priya Singh: Thanks everyone - we'll follow up in email.
[37:44] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcript has occasional mis-hearings (e.g., 'KV cash' vs 'KV cache', 'Redwood Dedicate' vs 'Redwood Dedicated'). Refer to shared docs for exact API examples.
